slides.title: Our route from evidence to action
slides.note: Click a section to jump to its opening. Section markers on subsequent slides keep the audience oriented.

slides.title: Rethinking Risk & Assurance
slides.note: Introduce Rethinking Risk and Assurance. The GRC integration gap: foundations, survey evidence and the opportunity for AI.

slides.title: Three disciplines. One purpose.
slides.note: These are three connected GRC disciplines selected for this seminar, not the expansion of the GRC acronym or an exhaustive list. Compliance and integrity remain foundational. Definitions are concise paraphrases: OCEG connects disciplines; COSO integrates risk with strategy and performance; the IIA distinguishes management responsibility from independent assurance. Balanced Scorecard and KPI practices operationalize performance; no claim that the three are a formal new standard.

slides.title: Shared goals. Disconnected decisions?
slides.note: Performance, risk and assurance share an objective but can remain disconnected in practice. Risk-to-goal: an increased exposure should inform whether the target remains achievable. Assurance-to-risk: serious audit evidence should challenge the assessment and the response. These are diagnostic questions, not a claim that the surveys measure Kemenkeu's performance.

slides.title: 89% did not report a unique strategic advantage.
slides.note: Read the displayed response level precisely. These are perceptions and separate survey questions, not an objective failure rate. Ask for a recent decision influenced by the risk process. Avoid turning the contrast into a causal or paired statistical test. International research motivates the local diagnostic question; it does not measure Kemenkeu. For a ministry, apply the question to public-service objective delivery rather than market competition.

links.label: NC State University ERM Initiative + AICPA · 2026 State of Risk Oversight ↗

slides.referenceContext: The 2026 NC State University ERM Initiative and AICPA survey gathered self-reported views from 331 executives and board-level leaders. Only 11% reported a unique strategic or competitive advantage from risk management; the displayed 89% is its rounded complement.
slides.narrativeConnection: The finding distinguishes having a risk process from obtaining strategic value. It supports asking whether risk information actually changes decisions about objectives. It does not establish that 89% of organizations failed at risk management or describe Kemenkeu specifically.

slides.title: 49% of business executives see an assurance alignment gap.
slides.note: Read the subgroup qualifier before the percentage. This item concerns perceived coordination with other lines. It is not a failure rate and does not show that a finding never influenced management. The three questions on the right are our proposed application, not questions asked by PwC.

links.label: PwC · Global Internal Audit Study 2023 · section 3 ↗

slides.referenceContext: PwC's 2023 Global Internal Audit Study examined the views of audit leaders, business and board respondents, and risk/compliance leaders. In the business-executive subgroup, 49% perceived that internal audit lacked strong alignment with other lines on key risks and problems.
slides.narrativeConnection: This is evidence of a perceived coordination gap between assurance and other management activities. It relates to whether audit evidence reaches risk owners and informs their response. It is not an audit failure rate, and the full study sample is not the denominator for this subgroup percentage.

slides.title: A report is not a decision
slides.note: Explain the mechanism behind the survey results: producing a risk report does not itself change a management decision or protect an objective. Agarwal and Kallapur describe disconnected reporting and compliance-oriented practices in qualitative field research. This is not a universal failure claim. Next, introduce AI support across the risk cycle and the opportunity to connect evidence to decisions.

links.label: Ruchi Agarwal and Sanjay Kallapur · Four Ways to Improve Risk Reporting (2021) ↗

slides.referenceContext: Agarwal and Kallapur's 2021 research examines how risk reporting can become disconnected from strategy and performance. Qualitative work in more than 20 large financial institutions identifies reporting practices treated as a compliance obligation rather than an input to management decisions.
slides.narrativeConnection: The research provides a mechanism for the gap shown in the preceding surveys: a report can be prepared and filed without changing assumptions, choices or responses. Its relevance is the need to connect risk information to decisions that protect objectives. It does not estimate the prevalence of this problem across all organizations.

slides.title: AI in Risk Management
slides.note: Open section two with AI assistance across the risk cycle. Then explain why risk connects performance and assurance, before introducing SIGNAL and the hands-on.

slides.title: AI can assist the whole risk cycle.
slides.note: All four phases and their explanations are visible at the same time. AI supports identification, assessment, treatment and monitoring; human authority remains central. The diagram distinguishes AI assistance from human validation, authorization and accountability at each phase. It is a capability argument, not a claim that the seminar app currently uses a language model.

slides.title: Better tools. Still disconnected?
slides.note: AI can improve individual tasks without fixing disconnected performance, risk and assurance processes. Following the survey evidence, ask whether better tools change a forecast, assessment or owned response in time to protect the objective. The next slide focuses on risk as the connection between performance and assurance; SIGNAL then turns this idea into a practical framework and hands-on exercise. This is a design proposition, not a measured universal failure rate.

slides.title: Risk management is the GRC choke point
slides.note: Risk management is the proposed connection point between performance and assurance: objectives define exposure; assurance challenges protection; the risk view should carry both into timely management decisions. The choke-point framing is our interpretation of the integration gap, not a survey finding.

slides.title: Signal Framework
slides.note: SIGNAL is presented as one complete path. The large acronym aligns with six explanations underneath. S-I-G-N uses AI to prepare evidence and advice; A-L foregrounds human decisions, action and verification. All phases remain visible. Human judgment can challenge relevance, assumptions and proposed actions throughout the path. This is the presenter's working framework, not an external standard.

slides.title: One organization. Two signal streams. A complete decision cycle.
slides.note: Invite participants to act as the organization leader. First examine risks and initial mitigation commitments, then activate news sources. Work one guided news item together before the independent review. Participants can reject a signal, retain a score, or customize a response with reasons. We then repeat with internal sources. Dashboard closes the loop. Participants use phones or computers; presenter uses separate admin controls.

slides.title: Join the session
slides.note: Presenter opens /admin in the same browser, creates a session, and pastes its LAN audience link here. All phones must reach the laptop. Participants need no account. If setup overruns, shorten the batch debrief rather than the first end-to-end decision.

slides.title: Which organization will you lead?
slides.note: These are fictional Indonesian organizations with strategic exposure. Logistics: export growth, corridor diversification and hub investment. Seafood exporter: export competitiveness and market concentration. Digital: AI differentiation, funded enterprise demand and regulated-market entry. All revenue weights and targets are exercise assumptions. Each objective has two supplied risks. Participants can rename their company and use random-fill aids.

slides.title: Your workspace. Three views.
slides.note: Introduce Dashboard, Risk Monitoring and Risk Trigger using three screenshots before any signal is released. Dashboard shows context and exposure; Risk Monitoring lists risks and mitigation commitments; Risk Trigger configures evidence sources. Do not introduce the alert yet.

slides.title: A trade-policy shock. Which growth plans are exposed?
slides.note: Show the original headline and opening article paragraphs side by side. Ask which strategic assumptions need review. This is the 2 April announcement as reported 3 April, replayed with an 8 April knowledge cutoff. Verify product coverage, timing, contracts and customers. Do not assume 32% equals a company revenue loss or applies to freight services. These are cropped screenshots of the original webpage, not a reconstructed article.

slides.title: Which organization is affected by this news?
slides.note: Show all three dependency explanations immediately. Compare the strong relevance for the two export-linked organizations with the absence of an established direct goods-tariff dependency for domestic software. Relevance is not severity: the owner must verify the exposure before changing the assessment.

slides.title: Now, open your alert.
slides.note: After discussing the news and which organization is exposed, direct participants to Risk Monitoring. Highlight 1 marks the menu, 2 the new alert count, and 3 the risk row. Click the row or its alert to open the connected response.

slides.title: The alert reaches your risk. You decide whether to capture it.
slides.note: Use the still image: read the original source and summary, challenge its relevance to the risk and objective, then accept or decline each signal. Decisions are drafts until the connected response is finished.

slides.title: A changed assumption can move the assessment
slides.note: P marks the previous position (likelihood 3, impact 4, score 12). S marks the proposal (likelihood 4, impact 4, score 16). Select a matrix cell, explain a custom or unchanged score, then use Save risk score at bottom right. The adjacent status identifies the choice. The score remains a draft until Finish.

slides.title: The action follows the exposed dependency
slides.note: Above the example tolerance of 12, a new mitigation is required. Accept the suggested action or create one. Set the owner, due date and expected reductions in likelihood and impact. The projection assumes effective delivery, which must later be verified.

slides.title: 16 before. 12 projected after.
slides.note: The assessed score is 16 (L4 x I4). A planned likelihood reduction of 1 and impact reduction of 0 produces projected residual 12 (L3 x I4), meeting the example tolerance. Finish saves all decisions together. Residual 12 is conditional on successful mitigation; the assessed 16 remains recorded.

slides.title: The dashboard shows decisions and commitments
slides.note: The dashboard and risk list show projected residual exposure. The new mitigation is listed with owner, deadline and expected effect. Decision history preserves the pre-mitigation assessment. Planned protection does not prove actual effectiveness.

slides.title: More signals. Better risk decisions.
slides.note: Release the wider external and internal signal batches. Participants can continue as risk managers while the presentation proceeds. Recap dynamic, responsive, connected and accountable decisions as intended design benefits, not measured outcomes. Transition from AI-assisted risk decisions to AI in assurance: AI helps auditors examine evidence, while auditors retain independent judgment. The SPIT/SIPT institutional direction comes after that assurance section.

slides.title: AI in Assurance
slides.note: Introduce AI in Assurance. AI-assisted assurance, AI oversight and supervisory technology.

slides.title: Assurance of AI. Assurance with AI.
slides.note: Bridge before the technical detail. Mengawasi AI means examining AI as a source of risk: intended use, data, validation, fairness, security, access, monitoring, vendor dependencies and a named accountable owner. Mengawasi dengan AI means using AI to assist oversight of activities and risks, including activities that do not use AI. These are complementary roles, not interchangeable terms. An AI supervisory tool itself belongs within AI governance. The next two slides explain the three layers of frontier AI risk and the scope of AI oversight before returning to SupTech.

links.label: OECD / Supervision of Artificial Intelligence in Finance (2026) ↗

slides.title: Assurance of AI
slides.note: AI as the object of assurance. Introduce the risks of AI systems and the evidence needed to assess their oversight.

slides.title: Three layers of frontier AI risk
slides.note: Source: presenter-supplied Understanding Frontier AI - IHT OJK 2026.pptx, displayed slide 26 / 64, Tiga layer risiko frontier AI. This training taxonomy distinguishes model behavior, malicious use of capabilities, and deployment or shared-dependency risk. The layers can overlap: a prompt-injection attack is malicious use that exploits the deployed system. Herding refers to correlated behavior when institutions rely on similar models or signals. This slide explains why AI is an object of oversight. Next: examine purpose, accountability, data, authority and monitoring across the system.

slides.title: Supervise AI: what must we examine?
slides.note: Source: presenter-supplied Understanding Frontier AI - IHT OJK 2026.pptx, displayed slides 48-50 / 64. This is a training synthesis, not a regulatory checklist. Human-in-the-loop: a person approves each consequential decision. Human-on-the-loop: a person monitors and can override within defined limits. Human-in-command: people set the permitted autonomy, guardrails and stop conditions; this can coexist with the other arrangements. The use-case owner owns outcomes and controls, risk/compliance challenges and monitors, and internal audit independently assesses governance and control effectiveness. Examine the deployed system, including vendor components, rather than model accuracy alone. Transition: AI used for supervision also needs this oversight. Continue to SupTech.

slides.title: Assurance with AI
slides.note: AI as an audit assistant. Transition from assessing AI systems to using AI to support audit work, while auditors retain judgment and accountability.

slides.title: SupTech: from more data to focused supervision
slides.note: Pengawasan menggunakan AI is an AI-enabled part of SupTech, not the definition of all SupTech. Financial authorities use the term for technology supporting supervision, including data collection and analytics; the organizational example here is an illustrative adaptation, not a regulatory classification. Potential uses include document extraction, anomaly detection, thematic analysis and prioritization. Outputs support rather than replace supervisory judgment: a flag is not proof of a violation or an automatic risk-score change. Require traceable sources, permitted data access, validation and monitoring of false positives and missed signals. Transition: what objectives, risks and controls give these signals meaning? That leads into performance, risk and assurance. SIGNAL demonstrates this decision workflow with transparent rules; no language model is connected.

slides.title: SupTech in practice: authorities using AI
slides.note: Five named authorities and their jurisdictions. European Central Bank: Athena document analysis and Heimdall questionnaire reading, in use as reported in November 2023; later generative features are not implied. Bank of England ? Prudential Regulation Authority: cognitive search introduced, as reported in October 2022, Box 3. Financial Conduct Authority: exploratory text analysis, predictive analytics and synthetic data in the same source. Australian Securities and Investments Commission: its official artificial intelligence transparency statement describes current analytics, compliance and fraud detection, and enforcement intelligence uses with human oversight. Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority: pre-inspection document analysis remained at proof-of-concept stage in June 2026. Locations describe supervisory jurisdictions, not headquarters. Status labels describe the cited publication, not a claim of universal deployment. Sources checked 21 October 2026. Close the assurance section by connecting AI-assisted evidence review and independent judgment to the earlier SIGNAL risk decisions. Next, explain how Kemenkeu is pursuing integrated control through SPIT and its SIPT information-system support.

slides.title: SIPT
slides.note: Bring the two AI applications together: dynamic risk management and AI-assisted assurance. Explain how SPIT and SIPT express Kemenkeu's direction toward integrated control and effective early warning. Distinguish intended RP/CMCA relationships from completed production AI integration.

slides.title: SIPT: connecting control information across Kemenkeu
slides.note: SIPT is the information-system support for SPIT, not another name for the framework. The expansion follows BaTii’s published strategy. The next slides explain the intended RP–CMCA direction supplied by the presenter; the public sources cited here do not establish production AI deployment. Participants may keep exploring the released signals while this section proceeds.

slides.title: Integrated Internal Control Framework (SPIT)
slides.note: Original standard framework exported directly from the presenter-supplied Framework SPIT.pptx using PowerPoint. Preserve all original labels and layout. Explain the foundation, proactive first line, integrated UKI and Itjen oversight, and system-supported real-time assurance. The application landscape includes Assurance Intelligence System, e-Profiling, CMCA, Risk Platform, Audit Management System and Integrity Platform. Next, focus on RP and CMCA as part of SIPT.

slides.title: One risk. One reference. Continuous assurance
slides.note: Presenter-supplied direction: RP becomes the single source of the risk register to enable one view of risk. Shared references connect evidence and assurance to objectives, risk owners and assessments. A consolidated view does not remove unit ownership or independent assurance. These are intended information relationships, not assertions about the current database schema or completed integrations. Shared risk context is the foundation for continuous assurance, not sufficient assurance by itself. The following slides explain monitoring, audit evidence, confirmation, action and verification.

slides.title: Continuous Monitoring & Continuous Audit
slides.note: CMCA means Continuous Monitoring & Continuous Audit. This conceptual direction distinguishes management monitoring of risk indicators and control exceptions from repeated auditor testing of evidence and controls for independent assurance. Both use the shared risk reference, while responsibility and independent judgment remain distinct. Continuous checks do not imply every control is tested in real time and do not replace deeper audit work. Next, explain owner confirmation before conclusions. This describes intended roles, not a completed system deployment.

slides.title: The review pattern: exception → confirmation → risk decision
slides.note: Conceptual CMCA flow: a risk-linked automated check surfaces an exception. Its data quality, rule scope and source records must be examined, then a responsible owner confirms whether the exception indicates meaningful exposure. Confirmed evidence can support risk reassessment; neither an exception nor confirmation automatically changes a risk score or constitutes an audit conclusion. Interfaces for SIPT and its platforms are outside this presentation. Evaluate risk implications and audit/control implications separately. Management owns risk decisions; auditors retain independent responsibility for assurance conclusions.

slides.title: A warning is effective when it changes a timely decision
slides.note: Assess outcomes rather than repeat the CMCA workflow. Timely: signals arrive before objectives are affected. Actionable: a named owner has a clear action and deadline. Verified: evidence shows the response works. RP provides shared context, CMCA supplies recurring checks, and confirmation validates anomalies. These criteria assess whether that flow protects objectives; alert counts alone are insufficient.
